Section 1: Week 48 Listening: A Study Group Meeting (Corrected)

Mia: Hi, Tom. Thanks for coming to this extra study group meeting. I know it's short notice, but I really appreciate you making the time.
Tom: No problem, Mia. I think we need it. The last practice test was tough, and I didn't feel prepared for some of the sections.
Mia: Exactly. I got a 5.5 in listening, but I need a 6.5 for my university application. So I'm focusing on listening this week and trying to improve my score as much as I can.
Tom: That's a big gap. I got 6.0 in listening, but my writing is only 5.5. I need 6.0 in writing, so I have to work on that too.
Mia: So we both have different weak areas. Maybe we can help each other and share our strengths.
Tom: Good idea. But first, let's review the mistakes from last week's test. I missed three questions because I didn't read the instructions carefully.
Mia: I missed two questions because I lost my place in the recording. I was still thinking about question 5 when question 6 started, so I couldn't catch the answer.
Tom: That happens to me too. I think we should practice predicting answers before we listen, so we know what kind of information to expect.
Mia: Yes, and we should also check our spelling. I wrote 'accommodation' wrong last time, which cost me a point.
Tom: Spelling is important. I wrote 'February' without the first 'r', and I lost marks for that as well.
Mia: Let's make a plan. We can meet twice a week: on Tuesday and Thursday evenings, if that works for you.
Tom: Tuesday is fine, but Thursday I have a class until 7 p.m. Can we meet at 7:30 instead?
Mia: Sure. Let's meet in the library on Tuesday at 6 p.m., and on Thursday at 7:30 p.m. in the coffee shop near the station.
Tom: The coffee shop might be noisy, and that could make listening practice difficult. How about the quiet room in the student center?
Mia: Good point. Let's meet in the quiet room on Thursday, then.
Tom: OK. What about materials? I have a practice book with six tests, so we can use that for reading and listening.
Mia: I have an online course with ten listening exercises. We can share, and that gives us plenty to work with.
Tom: Great. I'll bring my book on Tuesday. Can you send me the link to your online course?
Mia: Yes, I'll email it tonight. Also, we should do a full test under exam conditions once a week, so we get used to the timing.
Tom: Agreed. Let's do that on Saturdays. But not this Saturday, because I'm visiting my parents.
Mia: No problem. We can start next Saturday. Let's meet at 9 a.m. in the library.
Tom: 9 a.m. is a bit early for me. Can we make it 10 a.m.?
Mia: 10 a.m. works. I'll book a study room, so we have a quiet space.
Tom: Thanks, Mia. I feel more confident already, and I think this plan will really help.
Mia: Me too. See you on Tuesday.

Section 2: Community Garden Project: A Volunteer Briefing

Good morning, everyone. My name is Sarah, and I'm the coordinator of the Green Roots Community Garden. Thank you for coming to this volunteer briefing. Today I'll explain how the project works and what you need to know if you'd like to join.

First, a bit of background. The garden was started three years ago on a piece of unused land behind the library. At that time, it was just weeds and rubbish. A small group of neighbours decided to clean it up and turn it into a shared space. Now we have 25 individual plots, a communal herb bed, and a small orchard with apple and pear trees.

We rely entirely on volunteers. There are no paid staff. Each volunteer is asked to commit to at least two hours a week. You can choose your own hours, but most people come on Saturday mornings between nine and twelve. If you can't manage a regular weekly slot, that's fine—we also need help with one-off events like our summer fair.

Now, about the plots. If you want your own plot, there's a waiting list. Currently about 15 people are waiting, and the average wait is six months. However, you don't need a plot to volunteer. Many people just help with general maintenance—weeding, watering, and keeping the paths clear.

What should you bring? We provide tools like spades and forks, but you must bring your own gloves. We also recommend wearing sturdy shoes, as the ground can be muddy. There's a shed where you can store your tools if you become a regular volunteer.

Safety is important. We have a first-aid kit in the shed, and at least one trained first-aider is on site during organised sessions. If you're using the strimmer or the hedge trimmer, you must attend a short training session first. These run on the first Sunday of each month.

Finally, social events. We hold a monthly potluck lunch on the last Saturday of the month. Everyone brings a dish to share. It's a great way to meet other volunteers. Also, we have a children's plot where families can garden together. Children must be accompanied by an adult at all times.

If you're interested, please pick up a registration form from the shed. There's no fee to join, but we suggest a small donation of £5 a year to help with seeds and equipment. That's optional, though.

Thank you for listening. I'll now take any questions.

Section 3: Week 48 Listening: Speaking Workshop – Deep Discussion and Four Retests

TUTOR: Good morning, everyone. Today we’re focusing on speaking part 3: deep discussion. I want you to practise summarizing, comparing, speculating, and using conditionals and concessions. Let’s start with your self-review. Lin, you said you often hesitate when you need to summarize a long point. Can you give an example?

LIN: Yes. Last week, when I talked about online learning, I kept repeating the same idea. I didn’t know how to condense it. So I lost time.

TUTOR: Right. A good summary should capture the main idea and one or two key details. Try to avoid examples unless they are essential. Now, Chen, you mentioned comparing. What’s difficult for you?

CHEN: I find it hard to compare two things without sounding like a list. For instance, comparing city life and country life, I just say ‘city is busy, country is quiet’ and then stop.

TUTOR: You can use comparative structures like ‘whereas’ or ‘while’ to show contrast. Also, consider comparing on specific aspects, such as cost, environment, or opportunities. Mei, you wanted to work on speculation. What strategies have you tried?

MEI: I try to use ‘might’ or ‘could’, but I often forget and just say ‘maybe’. Also, I’m not sure how to speculate about the past.

TUTOR: For past speculation, use ‘might have + past participle’, e.g., ‘They might have decided to move for better jobs.’ Now, about conditionals and concessions: these are useful for balanced arguments. For example, ‘If governments invested more in public transport, traffic would decrease.’ That’s a second conditional. For concession, you can say ‘Although online courses are convenient, they require strong self-discipline.’ Notice the comma after the concession clause. Jun, you had a question about your own errors?

JUN: Yes, I recorded myself and noticed I often use ‘although’ and ‘but’ together, like ‘Although it was expensive, but I bought it.’ I know it’s wrong, but I do it when I’m nervous.

TUTOR: That’s a common mistake. Choose one: either ‘Although it was expensive, I bought it’ or ‘It was expensive, but I bought it.’ Now, let’s plan the four retests for next week. Each of you will do a four-minute retest focusing on one area. Lin, you’ll focus on summarizing. Chen, on comparing. Mei, on speculating. Jun, on conditionals and concessions. You’ll record your retest and then transcribe it to identify errors. After that, we’ll meet individually to review. Any questions?

LIN: Should we use a timer?

TUTOR: Yes, use a timer and aim for four minutes. Also, try to incorporate at least two target structures in each retest. For example, in your summary retest, you could include a conditional: ‘If I had more time, I would explain further.’ That shows range. Remember, the goal is not perfection but awareness. Now, let’s do a quick practice. I’ll give you a topic, and you’ll discuss it in pairs for two minutes, focusing on one structure. Topic: ‘Should university education be free?’ Off you go.

Section 4: The Art of Speculation: Grammar for Advanced Discussion

Good morning, everyone. Today we continue our series on advanced speaking skills, and our focus is on grammar for deeper discussion. Specifically, we'll look at four functions: summarizing, comparing, speculating, and expressing conditions and concessions. These are essential for part 3 of the speaking test, where you need to develop your answers. Let's begin with summarizing. When you summarize, you condense information. A useful structure is 'Overall, the main point is that...' or 'To sum up, we can say that...'. For example, if you've been discussing a complex issue, you might say, 'Overall, the key takeaway is that both sides have valid concerns.' This shows you can synthesize. Now, comparing. Comparisons are not just about 'more' or 'less'. You can use 'whereas', 'while', or 'compared to'. For instance, 'Whereas urban areas offer more job opportunities, rural areas provide a quieter lifestyle.' Notice the contrast. Also, you can compare using 'the same as' or 'similar to'. But be careful: 'similar to' is followed by a noun phrase, not a clause. So say 'similar to the previous point', not 'similar to what we said before'—though in informal speech, the latter is common. Moving on to speculating. Speculation is about guessing with evidence. Use 'may', 'might', 'could', or 'must' for different levels of certainty. For example, 'The rise in remote work might be due to advances in technology.' Or 'That must have been a difficult decision.' Notice 'must have been' for past deduction. You can also use 'It's likely that...' or 'It seems that...'. These are softer. Now, conditions and concessions. Conditions use 'if' or 'unless'. For example, 'If governments invest in public transport, traffic congestion could decrease.' Concessions use 'although', 'even though', 'while', or 'despite'. For instance, 'Although the policy was controversial, it eventually gained support.' Or 'Despite the initial criticism, the project succeeded.' Note that 'despite' is followed by a noun or gerund, not a clause. So 'despite the rain' is correct, but 'despite it rained' is wrong. Now, let's talk about reviewing your own errors. After a speaking practice, record yourself and listen for these structures. Ask: Did I summarize clearly? Did I compare accurately? Did I speculate appropriately? Did I use conditions and concessions correctly? A common mistake is overusing 'but' instead of 'although' or 'however'. Another is using 'if' when 'unless' is needed. For example, 'Unless you study, you will fail' means 'If you don't study, you will fail.' So be precise. To improve, keep a log of your errors and review them weekly. This week, focus on using at least three of these structures in your speaking. Remember, fluency comes with practice. That's all for today. Next week, we'll look at hedging language.
